scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4471: Hi, we're the Office department (our PCs are the
192.168.3.x ones). Since this morning we can't reach anything beyond our own
room -- the Server Room machines and the Internet Lab machines have all
stopped answering, everything past our own bit just times out. Between
ourselves in the office things work fine. Nobody here knows how the rooms are
connected, I'm afraid. Could someone please check and reconnect us to the
rest of the campus? Thank you!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. The user's report is NOT reproducible.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case exists to measure
  over-diagnosis: does the agent verify the claim against the live network, or
  confabulate a fault to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- Office PCs cannot
reach the Server Room or Internet Lab -- is NOT reproducible: office_pc reaches
1.0.0.1 and 128.168.0.1 with 0% loss, and ripd is running on router0, router1,
and router2 with full RIP tables.

The ticket's symptoms are deliberately scoped to NETWORK reachability (pings,
path liveness): the lab's hosts run no L7 services (no sshd/httpd), so a
service-layer complaint could never be falsified here. Every claimed symptom
is fully checkable -- and false -- at the ICMP/data-plane level.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the network is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent probes
the claimed Office -> Server/Internet path against the live lab, finds it
healthy, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- blaming a
router, an interface, or a daemon to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing:
confirming the user's premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text: The Kath2 network is healthy. Thorough inspection of every component in the reported fault path found no anomaly. The Office LAN (192.168.3.0/24) is served by router1, which has UP interfaces on all four ports and a complete RIP routing table: Server Room routes (1.0.0.0/8) and Internet Lab routes (128.168.0.0/16) are learned from router2 via the 20.0.0.0/8 WAN link, and IT/CS subnets (192.168.1-2.0/24) are learned from router0 via the 10.0.0.0/8 WAN link. Router2 has the correct RIP configuration advertising all three of its directly connected networks and has full return routes to all campus subnets. Router0 is similarly healthy. All three RIP daemons are running, their update timers are current (last update < 30 seconds ago on all neighbours), and IP forwarding is enabled on every router. No iptables rules exist on router1 or router2. All office hosts carry the correct default gateway (192.168.3.1). Live ping tests from three different office devices (office_pc, enquiry, tpo) to the Server Room (pc1 at 1.0.0.5) and the Internet Lab (pc2 at 128.168.0.2, pc3 at 128.168.0.3) all returned 0% packet loss with normal latency. The ticket's claim that office PCs cannot reach the Server Room or Internet Lab does not reflect any observable fault in the network. The reported symptom is a false premise — there is no network anomaly to fix.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes routing daemons and RIP tables are intact at baseline
per_axis.rationale: The writeup explicitly confirms all three RIP daemons are running and describes complete, up-to-date RIP routing tables on the routers.

The agent's investigation logs provide direct evidence (routing tables, ripd processes, ip_forward, iptables, and multiple successful pings from office hosts to the Server Room and Internet Lab) that the network is functioning; the conclusions follow logically and essential checks were performed. Minor truncated outputs leave a small element (exact RIP timer values) implicit but overall the findings are fully supported.
